Aristotle begins his examination of mathematical objects by first recalling the doctrine of sensible substances established earlier. He distinguishes two contrary opinions: one that mathematical objects exist as separate substances (the Platonic view), and another that they exist only in sensible particulars. Aquinas would approve Aristotle's rejection of Platonic mathematical Forms as self-subsisting entities. Mathematical objects are universal abstractions—lines, numbers, surfaces—that the intellect derives from sensible matter through a process of separation or precision (abstractio). They lack independent existence; they are beings of reason insofar as they are considered apart from the material singulars that instantiate them. Their truth consists in their correspondence to intelligible structure within created things, not in a transcendent realm. Aristotle's critique of the Platonists—that if mathematical objects subsisted separately, they could not account for the sensible world—reflects Aquinas's conviction that only God subsists apart from created multiplicity. All true being flows from act-as-such, and mathematical abstractions depend entirely on the actualized particulars from which intellect knows them.

Here Aristotle examines whether mathematical objects, even if they exist, could be separate substances. Aquinas reads this as a dialectical dismantling of the Platonic position. If numbers and geometric forms were truly separate from sensible bodies, they would need their own principles of being and change—yet they possess no such principles. Numbers do not come into being or pass away (at least not in the way sensible things do), nor do they interact causally with the physical world. This silence reveals the absurdity of the Platonic thesis. In Aquinas's terms: mathematical objects are indeed eternal and unchanging—precisely because they are not things-that-are-in-act in the strong sense. Rather, they represent structures *discovered* in being, patterns that intellect grasps when it abstracts from matter. The eternal character of mathematics thus reflects not a separate realm but the necessity of the logical relations among universals, which flow necessarily from the intelligible essences actualized in the sensible creation. To posit them as separate substances would multiply beings without necessity, violating the principle that being should not be predicated equivocally.

Aristotle pushes deeper: can mathematical objects be both universal *and* separate substances? For if they are universal (predicated of many particulars), how could they exist apart as individual substances? Conversely, if they are individual substances, how are they universal? This contradiction, Aquinas observes, follows necessarily from the Platonic error. It exposes the incoherence of the view that mathematical universals are self-subsisting things. Aquinas's own position is consonant here: universality belongs to concepts in the intellect and to natures considered as principles of predication—not to substances *as such*. A universal substance would be a contradiction in terms, a confusion of the order of being (ens) and the order of predicability (secundum praedicationem). Mathematical objects are universal in intellect because they abstract from singularizing matter; but their being—insofar as they have any being outside the mind—is grounded in the particulars that exemplify their structures. This chapter crystallizes why a medieval Christian metaphysician must reject the Platonic divinization of mathematical abstractions.

Aristotle examines the generation and corruptibility of mathematical objects. They appear neither to come into being nor to perish in any natural sense. But this, he suggests, is because they are not substances at all, only abstractions of the intellect. Generation and corruption belong to substances in act, which undergo motion and change through the agency of causes. Mathematical truths—that 2+2=4, that the angles of a triangle sum to 180°—do not come-to-be through any efficient cause; they are grasped as necessary consequences of the essences involved. Aquinas would emphasize that this timeless necessity of mathematical truth constitutes no argument for their subsistence. Rather, it shows that mathematics deals with intelligible essences, not with singular existents. The intellect knows these essences truly, but their truth is a truth *in the mind* (veritas in mente) reflecting structures present in the real world, not a proof of their independent being. The immutability of mathematical objects thus reflects the immutability of the divine intellect's knowing, in which all such truths are eternally present as divine ideas—not Plato's Forms, but God's exemplary knowledge.

Here the question becomes: if mathematical objects are neither substances nor generated, what is their ontological status? Aristotle clarifies that they are indeed real—there is genuine knowledge of them—but they exist *in sensible particulars*, abstracted by intellect. A line is not a self-subsisting entity; it is what intellect apprehends when it considers the extension of a sensible body. The universal applies to all such cases through the unity of the intelligible form. Aquinas finds here a vindication of his own doctrine of the universale in re (the universal existing in the thing). A nature or essence—even a mathematical one—has a real foundation in the particular, though its universality is a work of intellect. The ontology is: sensible substance (ens in actu); its intelligible structure (apprehended by abstraction); and the universal concept (formed in the intellect). None of these levels is false; all correspond to the graduated hierarchy of being that flows from God. Mathematical truth thus participates in the immutable truth of the divine mind, yet depends wholly on the creation of sensible particulars.

Aristotle turns to the question of divisibility and unity in mathematical objects. A line can be divided, yet we speak of unity in numbers and figures. How are these reconciled? The resolution lies in understanding what "unity" and "divisibility" mean at each level. In the sensible particular, continuous quantity admits of division without destruction of substance (a rod can be cut into pieces, each still real). In the mathematical abstraction, divisibility is a *conceptual* feature—the line is divisible in thought, meaning we can consider parts of it while grasping it as one form. This unity-in-divisibility reflects, in Aquinas's view, the deeper metaphysical truth that being itself embraces both unity and multiplicity, act and potentiality. God is pure Unity (actus purus), and all created being exhibits the tension between act (the unifying form) and potentiality (the divisible matter or substrate). Mathematics crystallizes this tension in intelligible form, showing how multiplicity and unity cohere. This chapter thus elevates mathematical discourse to a mirror of metaphysical structure.

Aristotle addresses the question of whether mathematical objects can be said to have matter. If they do, it would be intelligible matter, not sensible matter. Intelligible matter is the quantity or extension considered apart from sensible qualities—what remains when intellect abstracts from color, hardness, etc., focusing only on shape and size. Aquinas recognizes this doctrine of intelligible matter (materia intelligibilis) as a refinement crucial to understanding how abstraction works. Sensible particulars possess sensible matter (this wood, this bronze). When intellect abstracts, retaining quantity but setting aside sensible accidents, it grasps intelligible matter. Mathematical objects are thus forms of intelligible matter: a triangle in pure geometry is a form imposed on the intelligible matter of extension. This preserves the Aristotelian insight that even universals and abstractions have a quasi-material component (a principle of multiplicity) preventing them from collapsing into pure form. Once again, Aquinas sees the graduated ontology: sensible matter → intelligible matter → pure form (God). All reflect the fundamental act-potency structure of all being-other-than-God.

The question now: is a number one substance, or many substances? If the number "five" is a substance (the Pythagorean view), is it one substance or five? The incoherence reveals another angle of the Platonic error. Aquinas would note that this puzzle dissolves once we recognize that "five" is not a substance at all but a *universal concept*. The numeral five is one universal (the form or essence of fiveness) predicated of many quintuples, or—in a different sense—the unity of a single concept in the mind. Substance is always particular and concrete. Numbers abstract from singularity, so they cannot be substances. Yet numbers are *real* as objective logical relations grounded in created beings. The existence of five sheep demonstrates the real applicability of the number-concept; the concept "fiveness" is not a mere subjective invention but captures an intelligible feature of the sensible world. This chapter shows that Aristotle (and Aquinas) can grant full reality to mathematical knowledge without hypostatizing mathematics into a realm of Platonic Forms.

Aristotle examines the claim that points, lines, and surfaces are substances or components of substances. But these geometrical abstractions depend on sensible bodies for their intelligibility. A point exists only as the limit of a line; a line only as the limit of a surface; surfaces only as the bounds of bodies. Remove the sensible body (or at least the intellectual consideration of it), and these lower-dimensional entities have no independent being. This reflects Aquinas's hierarchy: a geometric point is less a being than the line that bounds it, which is less a being than the surface, which is less a being than the three-dimensional body. All are abstractions from the lowest level of abstraction—pure potentiality, or intelligible matter—which grounds them all. This exemplifies the general truth that in the order of abstract knowledge, the more abstract (the point) depends on the less abstract (the body), just as the accidental depends on the substantial. God alone is utterly independent; all creation exhibits this web of dependence, intelligibly reflected in the hierarchy of mathematical abstractions.

Aristotle concludes his analysis by affirming that mathematical objects, precisely because they are not substances, are secondary realities—beings-by-abstraction, not beings-in-act. Yet they are not false or merely subjective. They represent intelligible patterns in the sensible world, knowable with certainty because they capture necessary truths about quantity and structure that inhere in all created bodies. For Aquinas, this vindication of mathematical knowledge without Platonic realism completes the metaphysical vision: sensible substances are primary, containing within them intelligible essences; through abstraction, intellect grasps these essences as universals; mathematical objects are the purest expression of intelligible quantity, expressing truths that flow necessarily from the essences actualized in creation. This entire structure of knowing—from the sensible singular to the abstract universal to the intelligible necessity—reflects the overflow of divine wisdom into the creation. Mathematics thus becomes a hymn to the rational order God has inscribed in being itself.
